603.title: Jambavan wakes Hanuman
603.hook: the strongest one on the beach hasn't said a word, so an old bear sits down and tells him his own story; why Hindus still sing it back to him
603.carry: strength remembered: why Hindus sing the Chalisa
603.howItsDone: Jambavan reminding Hanuman of his strength is one of the best-loved scenes in Hindu storytelling, and many families sing the Hanuman Chalisa, which retells Hanuman's deeds, on Tuesdays and Saturdays or before something they're afraid of.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yojana. Ten, twenty, thirty, ninety, and satya: say what you can really do.

Some people never put their hand up. Not because they can't do the thing, but because it hasn't occurred to them that they could. On the beach, while the others called out their numbers, Hanuman sat to one side, silent. Valmiki doesn't give him a line in the whole count. So Jambavan, the oldest one there, the one who knows everybody's story, gets up, walks over, and sits down beside him.
screen: `HANUMAN SITS APART.` → `NOT ONE WORD IN THE COUNT.` → `JAMBAVAN WALKS OVER.`

segments.voice: Jambavan tells Hanuman his own story. Your mother was Anjana. Your father is Vayu, the wind. As a baby you saw the sun coming up, thought it was a ripe fruit, and jumped for it, straight into the sky. Indra, king of the gods, threw his thunderbolt, you fell, and your jaw was struck. In Sanskrit the jaw is hanu, and that's where your name comes from. Then Jambavan says what he came to say: you have your father's speed. Why are you sitting there? Hanuman stands up. Valmiki describes him growing, filling with strength, roaring until the others cheer. He climbs Mount Mahendra to push off from, and there the Kishkindha Kanda, the book of the monkey kingdom, ends: on a mountaintop, before the jump. Why did he need reminding? Valmiki doesn't fully say; a story in the last book, which many scholars think was added later, says sages made him forget his strength until someone recalled it. Here's what Hindus do with this scene. Jambavan woke Hanuman's strength by telling him his story, and families do the same in prayer. The Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses sung in Hindu homes everywhere, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, retells his deeds, the baby who took the sun for a sweet fruit among them. People sing it before exams, surgeries, long drives, whenever they're afraid. And many teachers read the beach as the soul's own story: the atman, the true self, is never weak, only forgetful, and a guru's work, like Jambavan's, is to remind it.

604.title: An arrow from Rama's bow
604.hook: the Sundara Kanda opens with Hanuman pressing a mountain until water runs from the rock, then going as Rama's arrow, not his own
604.carry: dasya: going as God's arrow, not your own
604.tomorrow: The trees that saw him off
604.howItsDone: Many Hindus recite the Sundara Kanda in full at home or in temples, often over several days, and some families read it in times of difficulty or before a new undertaking; Hanuman is the classic picture of dasya, devotion as service.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hanu. Jambavan told Hanuman his own story, the way the Chalisa still does, and Hanuman stood up and climbed Mount Mahendra.

Of the seven books of the Ramayana, this is the one many Hindu families read on its own, start to finish, sometimes over days, sometimes when life is hard. It's the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book. And it begins mid-breath. The first verse opens, tato rāvaṇanītāyāḥ sītāyāḥ śatrukarśanaḥ: then, the tamer of enemies, of Sita, carried off by Ravana. It goes on: he set out to find her trail, along the path the sky-travelers use. No warm-up. Just: then.
screen: `THE BOOK MANY FAMILIES READ WHOLE.` → `SUNDARA: THE BEAUTIFUL BOOK.` → `IT BEGINS WITH 'THEN.'`

segments.voice: Hanuman stands on Mahendra, and Valmiki slows everything down. Hanuman presses his hands and feet into the mountain. The rock gives. Streams burst out of it. Animals bolt from their caves, and sages and celestial beings rise into the air to get out of the way. A whole mountain shakes because one being is gathering himself. Then Hanuman says what he'll do. He'll go to Lanka like an arrow loosed from Rama's bow. If Sita isn't there, he'll search heaven. Then he crouches, draws in his breath, and springs. Notice the comparison he chooses. Not a bird, not the wind, though he's the wind's son. An arrow from Rama's bow: he isn't going for himself; he's the shot Rama is firing across the sea. This is why Hindus hold Hanuman up as the great example of dasya, devotion as a servant, one of the nine ways of bhakti the Bhagavata lists. And the servant here isn't small. He's the strongest being in the story, and he points all of it at someone else's purpose. Krishna says it in the Gita too: whatever you do, offer it to me. So many Hindus, before work, a test or a meal, quietly offer it to God, and some say after: Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna. Why is the book called beautiful? Valmiki never says, and people give different answers. One many tell: it's where hope returns. The story was stuck on a beach. Now it moves.

605.title: The trees that saw him off
605.hook: the trees on Mahendra fly after Hanuman like family seeing off a traveler; why Hindu families walk you out and bless you
605.carry: ashirvad: a blessing goes where family can't
605.howItsDone: Many Hindu families still walk a departing guest or traveler out, and before journeys and exams children touch elders' feet for ashirvad; devotional paintings often show Hanuman in midair over the sea with flowers falling around him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman sprang like an arrow from Rama's bow. That's dasya: going as God's arrow, not your own.

Valmiki gives Hanuman's leap an escort. The force of his takeoff tears the flowering trees on Mahendra loose, and they fly up after him. It's a picture from ordinary life, borrowed for a mountain: the parent at the school gate, the one who comes as far as they can and then has to stop. Hanuman is about to cross a hundred yojanas alone, and the trees go with him as far as trees can.
screen: `THE TREES FLY AFTER HIM.` → `AS FAR AS THEY CAN GO.`

segments.voice: Valmiki makes the comparison himself: the trees follow Hanuman for a while like relatives seeing off someone dear, and then, one by one, they drop into the ocean, and their blossoms float on the dark water like stars. Then he turns to Hanuman: arms outstretched, eyes shining, his shadow moving over the waves like a ship under sail. And the gods, the celestial singers and the great sages watch from the sky and shower him with flowers and praise. Valmiki didn't need to explain the picture of relatives turning back. His listeners knew it, and the epic shows it elsewhere: when Rama leaves for exile, the people of Ayodhya follow his chariot until they can't. It's a Hindu courtesy still kept. You walk them to the door, the gate, the car, and you send them with a blessing. That blessing has a name: ashirvad. Before a journey, an exam or a wedding, many Hindus touch an elder's feet, and the elder's hand comes down on their head. Some families add a spoonful of curd and sugar for a good start. The idea under it, as many families put it: a blessing goes where the family can't. And Hanuman himself lived it. Before he leapt, Valmiki says, he folded his hands and bowed to the Sun, to Indra, to Brahma, and to his father the Wind. The trees fell. The flowers from the sky kept coming. Hanuman crosses alone, but he doesn't cross unblessed.

606.title: Mainaka rises from the sea
606.hook: halfway across the sea, a golden mountain rises and offers Hanuman rest; how to honor a gift and keep a vow
606.carry: sankalpa: Rama's work first, then rest
606.howItsDone: In Sundara Kanda recitations, Mainaka is the first of the meetings over the sea, and Tulsidas's line 'until Rama's work is done, where is rest for me?' is one many devotees know by heart; many families also keep a Tuesday fast for Hanuman.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the trees saw Hanuman off, and your line: ashirvad, a blessing goes where family can't.

You're driving a long way, late, and a friend texts: you're passing my town, come in, I've made dinner, sleep here. It's a real kindness. But if you stop, you won't get where you're going in time. That's the first test Hanuman meets over the ocean, and it isn't a monster. It's a gift. The sea has been watching him, and the sea feels it owes him something.
screen: `COME IN, I'VE MADE DINNER.` → `THE FIRST TEST IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's telling, the Ocean is a person who thinks and remembers, and it remembers a debt. Long ago King Sagara, an ancestor of Rama's own line, had sons who dug out the bed of the sea; tradition says that's why the ocean is called sagara. So the Ocean thinks: this monkey is on an errand for Rama, of the family that made me what I am. He shouldn't wear himself out. It calls to a mountain hidden beneath its waves, Mainaka, to rise and give the traveler a place to rest. Mainaka lifts out of the water, golden peaks shining, and invites Hanuman to rest, eat fruit, and then go on. Hanuman's first reaction is suspicion, and he pushes the mountain aside with his chest. Then Mainaka explains, and Hanuman answers with great courtesy: I'm grateful; your welcome is as good as done. But time is pressing, and I've promised not to stop. He touches the mountain with his hand and flies on. Tulsidas, retelling the scene centuries later in his Ramcharitmanas, gives Hanuman a line many families know by heart: Ram kaju kinhe binu mohi kahan bishram. Until Rama's work is done, where is rest for me? That's sankalpa: a vow made before God, which comes before comfort. Hindus make one at the start of a puja or a fast, saying what they'll do and why. And Hanuman shows how to keep it kindly. No lecture, no resting a little to be polite. He honors the gift with a touch, and keeps the vow.

607.title: Why Mainaka helped
607.hook: once, the story goes, mountains had wings, and one of them owes its wings to Hanuman's father; the Hindu idea of debts carried across generations
607.carry: rina: a debt of kindness comes due
607.howItsDone: The story of the winged mountains and Indra's thunderbolt is told in several Hindu texts, and the idea of debts to the gods, the sages and the ancestors is still taught, especially when families make shraddha offerings for their dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mainaka offered rest, and Hanuman touched the mountain and kept his sankalpa: Rama's work first.

Sometimes a stranger is kind to you, and later you find out why. Your grandmother taught their mother to read. Your dad once pulled their car out of a ditch in the snow. The kindness was a thank-you that had waited years for someone from your family to come along. When Mainaka rises from the sea, the Ocean has one reason to help. Mainaka, it turns out, has his own.
screen: `A STRANGER'S KINDNESS, EXPLAINED.` → `A THANK-YOU THAT WAITED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Mainaka tells Hanuman a story from the earliest age of the world. In those days, he says, the mountains had wings. They flew wherever they pleased, and the sages and creatures below lived in fear one would come down on them. So Indra, king of the gods, took up his thunderbolt and cut off their wings one after another. When Indra came for Mainaka, the wind god Vayu swept him out of reach and dropped him safely into the ocean, wings and all. Vayu, Mainaka reminds Hanuman, is your father. So I owe you. Helping you is how I pay your father back. Hold that next to yesterday. The Ocean helps because of Rama's ancestors; Mainaka helps because of Hanuman's father. Two old debts, coming due on the same crossing. Hindu teaching has a word for this: rina, debt. Old Vedic texts say every person is born owing three: to the gods, to the sages who handed down knowledge, and to the ancestors, repaid with worship, with study, and with raising a family. Hindus still honor the last one at shraddha, the offerings made for those who've died. And there's a last turn. Indra, the very god who cut the mountains' wings, is pleased at what Mainaka has done for Rama's messenger, and grants him safety. That's karma, the teaching that actions bear fruit, told not as a law but as a scene. A breath of wind long ago means a resting place today.

608.title: Surasa's open mouth
608.hook: the gods decide to test Hanuman, and send the mother of serpents with her mouth wide open; why Hindus pray to him for wisdom too
608.carry: bal and buddhi: strength and wisdom together
608.howItsDone: Storytellers telling the Sundara Kanda often pause on Surasa's growing mouth before revealing how Hanuman gets through, and many Hindu students say the Chalisa's 'bal buddhi bidya' line before exams.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mainaka repaid an old debt to the wind's son. Rina: a debt of kindness comes due.

A coach who keeps raising the bar every time you clear it. Some tests aren't trying to stop you; they're trying to see what you do when force won't work. Over the open sea, Mainaka behind him, Hanuman flies straight into one of those. And the ones who set it up aren't his enemies. They're the gods, who want to know what this monkey is really made of.
screen: `THE BAR KEEPS RISING.` → `THE GODS SET THE TEST.`

segments.voice: The gods, the celestial musicians and the great sages talk it over. They ask Surasa, the mother of the nagas, the serpent beings, to take a terrifying form and block Hanuman's way, so they can see his strength and his cleverness. Surasa rises from the sea: the gods have given you to me as food, she says. You have to enter my mouth. Hanuman doesn't attack. He talks. He tells her who he is and why he's here: Rama, Sita taken, the search. Then he makes a remarkable offer. Let me find Sita and tell Rama, and I promise I'll come back and enter your mouth. Surasa refuses. She has a boon, she says, that no one can get past her. And she opens her mouth. So Hanuman grows to ten yojanas, too big to swallow. She opens wider, twenty. He grows to thirty; she opens to forty. On they go, until her mouth gapes a hundred yojanas wide. Every time he gets bigger, she gets bigger. Remember why the gods sent her: to see his strength and his buddhi, his intelligence. That pairing is why Hanuman is prayed to the way he is. Near its opening, the Hanuman Chalisa asks him: bal buddhi bidya dehu mohi. Give me strength, wisdom and learning. Hindu students say that line before exams, and grandparents say it over them. Strength alone has only made Surasa's mouth bigger. Hanuman, hovering there, has to think of something else.
screen: `THE GODS ASK SURASA TO TEST HIM.` · `HANUMAN TALKS FIRST.` · `HE GROWS; SHE GROWS.` · `BAL, BUDDHI, BIDYA.` · then, large: `STRENGTH ISN'T ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: If you know it, say quietly the line many students say before an exam: bal buddhi bidya dehu mohi. Strength, wisdom, learning. Breathe in on bal, hold on buddhi, breathe out on bidya. If you'd rather not pray, bring to mind one problem where pushing harder keeps making it worse, let the breath get smaller and slower, and ask what wisdom would do instead.

609.title: Thumb-sized Hanuman
609.hook: with her mouth a hundred yojanas wide, Hanuman wins by becoming the size of a thumb and bowing; why the strongest god kneels
609.carry: make the ego small: Hanuman bows
609.howItsDone: Many Hindu tellers, from grandparents to temple storytellers, use Surasa's test to show that Hanuman's wisdom matters as much as his strength; temple images often show him kneeling at Rama's feet with folded hands, and devotional art shows the tiny Hanuman beside her vast mouth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Surasa's mouth grew every time Hanuman did, and the gods were watching for bal and buddhi, strength and wisdom.

Out over the open sea, a monkey grown to the size of a mountain hangs in the air. In front of him, a serpent mother's jaws gape a hundred yojanas wide. Every time he has grown, Surasa's mouth has grown wider, and the gods are watching. He's been answering size with size. Now, Valmiki says, in the blink of an eye, he does the opposite.
screen: `A MOUTH A HUNDRED YOJANAS WIDE.` → `SIZE AGAINST SIZE.` → `IN A BLINK, THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman makes himself tiny, about the size of a thumb. He darts into Surasa's enormous mouth and, before she can close it, darts back out. Then he stops in the air, bows, and speaks respectfully. I've entered your mouth, so your boon is kept. Now I'm going on to find Sita. He hasn't broken her rule or his promise to Rama. Both are kept at once. Surasa is delighted. She sets aside the frightening form, appears as herself, and blesses him: go, find Sita, bring her and Rama together. The gods who set the test cheer. Many teachers read the scene this way: the ego, ahamkara, answers size with size, and that contest never ends. The devotee gets through by becoming small and bowing. It's why the strongest being in the Ramayana is so often pictured kneeling at Rama's feet, hands folded. The Chalisa praises him for it: a tiny form to show himself to Sita, a terrible form to burn Lanka. He knows which one the moment needs. Look back at the week of crossings. Jambavan told Hanuman his own story, as the Chalisa still does. He went as Rama's arrow: dasya. The trees saw him off: ashirvad. He kept his sankalpa past Mainaka, who was repaying an old rina. And with Surasa: strength, wisdom, and an ego small enough to bow. One more meeting waits over the sea, and it is not a test.
screen: `HANUMAN BECOMES THUMB-SIZED.` · `IN AND OUT; HER BOON IS KEPT.` · `SURASA BLESSES HIM.` · `AHAMKARA: THE EGO, MADE SMALL.` · then, large: `THE STRONGEST ONE BOWS.`

segments.voice: Fold your hands and bow your head a little, the way Hanuman bowed to Surasa, and the way many Hindus bow before a murti. Let your breathing become small and quiet: shoulders soft, no need to take up extra room. If a thought pushes in, don't push back; let it pass through. If you'd rather not bow to God, bow to the day. Small, quiet, awake.
